newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel easing closure of West Bank and Gaza Strip.
newsitem.headline: Israel easing closure of West Bank and Gaza Strip.

text.p: Israel eased its crippling closure of the West Bank and Gaza Strip and a U.S. peace mediator announced a change of venue for troubled talks on Israeli troop redeployment from the city of Hebron.

"Beginning this Sunday, about 35,000 workers from Judea, Samaria (the West Bank) and Gaza will be permitted to work in Israel and all internal closures in Judea and Samaria will be lifted, except for the city of Nablus," said a spokesman for Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai on Thursday.

Some 60,000 Palestinians from the West Bank and the Gaza Strip worked in Israel before Moslem suicide bombings in February and March prompted Israel to stop most of them from coming in. The closure was then gradually eased.
About 19,500 Palestinians worked in Israel before last month's violence that killed 60 Arabs and 15 Jews and led to an Israeli blockade of the Gaza Strip and West Bank cities.

"The defence minister decided to ease significantly the closure on the territories in order to reduce the hardship of the Palestinian population...and the Palestinian economy," the spokesman said in a statement.

The announcement was made against the backdrop of U.S.-brokered negotiations on a partial Israeli pullout in Hebron, home to 400 Jews and 100,000 Palestinians, which Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said had achieved nothing.

U.S. Special Mideast Coordinator Dennis Ross, mediating the talks, said Israel and the PLO had agreed to move the negotiations from Gaza to the Red Sea resorts of Eilat, in Israel, and Taba, in Egypt.

"The parties agreed that in order to make continous, to intensify and to accelerate their discussions, the various committees would begin meeting on Monday, October 14 on a rotating basis in Taba and Egypt," he said in a statement.

Spurred by a White House summit after last month's clashes -- the most serious Israeli-Palestinian violence since peace deals were signed in 1993 -- the negotiations began on Sunday on Israel's proposals to step up security for settlers.
Palestinians have accused Israel of trying to reopen a Hebron troop redeployment agreement signed by the previous Labour-led government.

"What we seek in Hebron are security arrangements which are completely compatible with the peace deal," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a speech to Israeli executives in Tel Aviv. "They have nothing to do with reopening the agreements."
In the self-ruled city of Ramallah on Thursday, Arafat met representatives of 40 international donor countries and appealed for their "urgent help" in salvaging an economy badly hit by the closure.
"One-third of the population is living in absolute misery," Salam Fayyad, the International Monetary Fund representative in the Palestinian areas, told the conference.
Mohammad Shtayeh, director of the Palestinian Economic Council for Development and Reconstruction (PECDAR), estimated the closure had cost the Palestinian economy $8 million a day.
It was unclear how long it would take Israel to carry out security checks and issue work permits to 35,000 labourers.
Asked about the Israeli announcement, Major General Abdelrazeq al-Majayda, commander of Palestinian police forces in Gaza, told Reuters: "We were not informed about this. We have no idea."
Mordechai's spokesman said the defence minister had also ordered the opening of two Gaza crossings, Karni and Sufa, for the passage of goods in and out of the Strip.

But he said Israeli reinforcements, rushed to the West Bank and Gaza after Netanyahu's opening of an archaeological tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem touched off the clashes, would remain to provide "a suitable response to any development".
